title: Week 2 quiz: Prompt, retrieve, or train?

questions.prompt: Ovadia et al. (2023) compared continued training on raw text with retrieval for adding knowledge to 7B open models. Which summary matches their results?

options.text: Fine-tuning beat retrieval on new knowledge, and retrieval beat fine-tuning on knowledge the model had already seen.
options.rationale: They found retrieval better in both cases.

options.text: Retrieval consistently beat fine-tuning, and training on many paraphrases of each fact narrowed the gap somewhat.
options.rationale: Yes. On their current-events set, retrieval scored far higher, and paraphrase augmentation helped the fine-tuned models.

options.text: The two were statistically indistinguishable on every task.
options.rationale: The gaps were large, for example roughly 0.88 with retrieval versus roughly 0.50 after fine-tuning for Mistral 7B on current events.

options.text: Combining retrieval and fine-tuning was always best.
options.rationale: In their setup, adding fine-tuning to retrieval did not beat retrieval alone.

questions.explanation: Facts belong in the context, where you can update and cite them. A single pass over a document teaches a model little; even ten paraphrases left fine-tuning well behind retrieval in this study.

questions.prompt: Your prompted extraction feature costs about $0.018 per request on a large model and handles 30,000 requests a month. A small fine-tuned model would cost about $0.0004 per request, but the dataset, training, and evals would cost about $24,000 up front, plus $1,500 a month to monitor and re-evaluate. Amortizing over 12 months, break-even is about 200,000 requests a month. Leadership asks whether to fine-tune now. What do you recommend?

options.text: Fine-tune now: the per-request cost is 45 times lower.
options.rationale: The per-request ratio ignores fixed costs. At 30,000 requests the prompted model costs about $540 a month; the fine-tuned path costs about $3,500.

options.text: Keep the prompted model, record the break-even analysis, and revisit if volume approaches the break-even point or a latency target forces the issue.
options.rationale: Yes. The analysis says fine-tuning loses money at current volume. Writing it down makes the trigger for revisiting explicit.

options.text: Fine-tune now because the base model of the small model will last forever once trained.
options.rationale: Fine-tuned models go away with their base model. The amortization period should reflect the base model's expected life, which argues for a shorter horizon, not a longer one.

options.text: Switch to the cheapest large model without measuring, since cost is the only issue.
options.rationale: Changing models is a reasonable option, but only with an eval run showing quality holds.

questions.explanation: Cost motives for fine-tuning are real above a volume threshold and imaginary below it. Include one-time and recurring costs, and the base model's lifetime, in the comparison.

questions.prompt: As of the lesson's review date, which statement about fine-tuning Claude is accurate?

options.text: Any current Claude model can be fine-tuned through the Claude API.
options.rationale: The lesson found no fine-tuning option for current Claude models in Anthropic's API documentation.

options.text: The only hosted Claude fine-tuning was Claude 3 Haiku on Amazon Bedrock, and that model has since been retired, so current Claude models are steered with prompts, structured outputs, and retrieval instead.
options.rationale: Yes. Bedrock's lifecycle page shows Claude 3 Haiku entering Legacy (no new fine-tuning jobs) in March 2026 and reaching end of life in September 2026 in the Region where fine-tuning ran.

options.text: Claude fine-tuning is available on Google Cloud but not on Bedrock.
options.rationale: The lesson's sources describe Claude fine-tuning only on Bedrock, for Claude 3 Haiku.

options.text: Claude models can be fine-tuned locally because their weights are open.
options.rationale: Claude's weights are not published. Open-weight models are the ones you can fine-tune yourself.

questions.explanation: Hosted fine-tuning of closed models has been shrinking (OpenAI is winding its platform down, Mistral's is deprecated, the Gemini API has no tunable model). A product that depends on a hosted fine-tune depends on that provider's roadmap; open-weight models trained with LoRA are the durable path this studio teaches.

questions.prompt: Which of these problems are good candidates for fine-tuning rather than retrieval? Select all that apply.

options.text: A model that keeps adding a friendly preamble before the JSON your parser expects, despite clear instructions
options.rationale: Format and behavior: fine-tuning's home ground (though structured outputs may solve it more cheaply).

options.text: Answering questions about this quarter's pricing changes
options.rationale: That's knowledge that changes. Retrieve it.

options.text: Writing support replies in your team's house style and length
options.rationale: Style is something fine-tuning learns well from examples.

options.text: A small model that must match a large model's accuracy on one narrow classification task at a fraction of the cost
options.rationale: Narrow-task accuracy and cost are standard reasons to fine-tune, often by distilling from the larger model.

options.text: Knowing the details of a customer contract signed last week
options.rationale: New, specific facts belong in the context. Fine-tuning on them invites confident errors.

questions.explanation: Ask what is missing. Missing or changing facts call for retrieval; persistent behavior, format, style, or a cost target on a narrow task can call for fine-tuning. Try prompting and structured outputs first, since they are cheaper to change.

questions.prompt: This check is meant to flag training examples where the gold answer was pasted into the prompt. What is wrong with it?

options.text: Nothing; it flags exactly the leaked examples.
options.rationale: Look at which messages the loop compares against.

options.text: It compares the answer against every message, including the assistant message itself, so every example is flagged.
options.rationale: Yes. The answer is always a substring of itself. Compare only against the messages before the last one (system and user turns).

options.text: It should use == instead of in, because a leak means the whole prompt equals the answer.
options.rationale: A leak is the answer appearing inside a longer prompt, so a substring check is right; it just needs the right messages.

options.text: strip() makes the check miss every leak.
options.rationale: Stripping whitespace from the answer only makes the substring check more robust.

questions.explanation: Write a test with a known-good example before trusting any validator. A check that flags everything is as useless as one that flags nothing, and it trains people to ignore it.

questions.prompt: A stratified split puts round(n * 0.15) records from each stratum into the test set. Three document kinds have 11, 7, and 3 records. What does this print?

options.rationale: 1.65 rounds to 2, 1.05 to 1, and 0.45 to 0. The smallest kind gets no test examples at all.
0.45 rounds down to 0, not up to 1.
1.65 rounds to 2.
round() with one argument returns an int.

questions.explanation: Small strata can vanish from the test set entirely, which means you'd report a score with no evidence about that kind of document. Set a minimum per stratum (or label more of the rare kind) and report per-stratum results separately.

questions.prompt: Your team wants to label 2,000 internal IT tickets with a GPT model through your company's OpenAI API account, then train an internal ticket-routing classifier that will never be distributed outside the company. A colleague says OpenAI's terms forbid any use of outputs for training. Based on the public OpenAI Services Agreement described in lesson 5, what is the best response?

options.text: The colleague is right: any training on outputs is forbidden.
options.rationale: The public agreement restricts developing models that compete with OpenAI, and defines a Permitted Exception for internal classifiers that aren't distributed.

options.text: The plan resembles the agreement's Permitted Exception for internal, non-distributed classifiers, but confirm with legal against the agreement that governs your account, record provenance, and review the labels.
options.rationale: Yes. The text supports the plan, but your account may be under a different agreement, and labels drafted by any model still need verification.

options.text: Terms don't apply to internal tools, so no review is needed.
options.rationale: Terms apply to all use of the service; internal use is one of the factors in this specific exception.

options.text: Switch providers, because every provider forbids this.
options.rationale: The providers' restrictions are worded differently, and this one has an explicit exception that may cover the plan.

questions.explanation: Read the actual clause, notice its exceptions, and still involve legal for the agreement you're under. Separately, treat model-drafted labels as drafts until people review them.

questions.prompt: Why do you need a validation split separate from the test split?

options.text: Because trainers require exactly three files.
options.rationale: Many trainers accept only a training file. The reason is statistical, not technical.

options.text: Because choosing checkpoints, epochs, or data changes on a split biases that split's score upward, so you need an untouched split to report.
options.rationale: Yes. Selecting the best of several noisy measurements overestimates the winner. The validation split absorbs that bias.

options.text: Because the validation split should contain harder examples than the test split.
options.rationale: Both should be drawn from the same distribution as production.

options.text: Because test sets are only used to compute loss, not accuracy.
options.rationale: Test sets are for the reported metrics.

questions.explanation: Iterate on validation, report on test. Early stopping (which limited harm in the new-knowledge study) is itself a choice made on validation data.

questions.prompt: This function assigns each record to a split. Each record has an id and a thread (several records can share a thread). What problem will the resulting splits have?
questions.code:
import hashlib

def split_of(record):
    h = int(hashlib.sha256(record["id"].encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 100
    return "test" if h < 15 else "val" if h < 30 else "train"

options.text: None; hashing makes the assignment random and reproducible, which is all a split needs.
options.rationale: Reproducible, yes. But related records are assigned independently.

options.text: Records from the same thread can land in different splits, so the model can see part of a test thread during training.
options.rationale: Yes. Hash the thread (the group), not the record id, so whole threads move together.

options.text: The split is not deterministic between runs.
options.rationale: sha256 of the id is deterministic.

options.text: Every record lands in train.
options.rationale: The modulo spreads records across all three splits.

questions.explanation: Group-aware splitting means the unit of assignment is the group. Ask what production looks like (new threads, new customers, new documents) and group by that.

questions.prompt: You are preparing support tickets as fine-tuning data. Which statements about PII and consent are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fine-tuned models can memorize and reproduce training text, so PII in examples can reach anyone who queries the model.
options.rationale: Carlini et al. extracted verbatim training data, including PII, from GPT-2, and fine-tuning repeats your examples over several epochs.

options.text: If a customer asks for deletion, removing their row from the JSONL file removes their data from the trained model.
options.rationale: Weights don't forget on request. The practical answer is to retrain from corrected data, so keep the build reproducible.

options.text: Data collected to resolve tickets is not automatically licensed for training; contracts, privacy notices, and law decide, with your privacy and legal teams.
options.rationale: Yes. Purpose and consent are part of the dataset's documentation.

options.text: Masking tools such as Presidio make manual checking unnecessary.
options.rationale: They help, but measure what they miss on your data before relying on them.

questions.explanation: Minimize what goes in, document why you may use it, store the training file like production data, and keep the pipeline reproducible so you can rebuild without someone's data.
